chapters.title: Chapter 2: Covariance, Correlation, and the Mathematics of Diversification

lessons.title: Covariance and Correlation: Measuring How Assets Actually Move Together

children.text: The last lesson ended with a promise: the 0.32 correlation between TCS and Maruti Suzuki was stated, not shown. Here is exactly how that number gets calculated, using the same six months of data, so you can check it with your own hands rather than take it on faith.

body.text: Covariance tells you the DIRECTION two assets tend to move together. Correlation takes that same information and rescales it into a clean, comparable number between -1 and +1. Every portfolio risk formula from here on runs through one of these two numbers.

body.caption: Covariance: the average product of each asset's deviation from its own mean, in the same period.

markDefs.definition: A measure of the tendency of two assets' returns to move together, calculated as the average product of their deviations from their own means in the same period. Positive when they tend to move in the same direction, negative when they tend to move in opposite directions.

children.text: Read the formula as a sign-counting exercise before anything else. In any given month, if both stocks sit above their own average return, the product of their two deviations is positive. If both sit below their own average, two negatives multiply to a positive as well. Only when one stock is above its average and the other is below does the product turn negative. Average that product across every month, and you get
: a running scorecard of whether two assets tend to have their good and bad months together, or apart.
Worked Example: TCS and Maruti Suzuki, Finally Solved

body.caption: Deviations and their product, TCS (mean 0.5%) and Maruti Suzuki (mean 0.5%)

children.text: The six products sum to 6.5. Divide by 6 months, and the covariance between TCS and Maruti Suzuki is 1.0833, in units of percent-squared. Month 4 alone, where both stocks fell together, contributes 8.75 of that 6.5 total on its own, since a shared bad month produces the largest positive product in the table. Notice the covariance is positive overall, but three of the six months (2, 5, and 6) contributed negative products, where one stock rose while the other fell. Covariance is a net score across all six months, not a claim that every month agreed.

body.label: Cov(TCS, Maruti Suzuki)
body.context: Positive, meaning the two stocks have a net tendency to move in the same direction, though far from a strict one.

body.text: Percent-squared is not an intuitive unit, exactly the same problem variance had back in Lesson 2. A covariance of 1.08 tells you the SIGN of the relationship clearly, but it is nearly impossible to judge, on its own, whether 1.08 counts as a strong or a weak relationship. That is what correlation fixes.

body.caption: Correlation: covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations. Always between -1 and +1.

children.text: Dividing covariance by both standard deviations strips out the units and the scale entirely, so the result always lands between -1 and +1, no matter how volatile the underlying stocks are. From Lesson 2, TCS's standard deviation is 1.7078% and Maruti Suzuki's is 1.9791%. Dividing the covariance of 1.0833 by the product of those two, 1.7078 x 1.9791 = 3.38, gives a correlation of 0.3205, or 0.32.

body.label: Correlation(TCS, Maruti Suzuki)
body.context: The exact number promised at the end of the previous lesson, now fully derived from the same six months of data.

body.code:
import numpy as np

# Same six months from the Chapter 1 case study
tcs = np.array([2, -1, 3, -2, 1, 0])
maruti = np.array([1, 2, 1, -3, -1, 3])

# ddof=0 to match the population formulas used throughout this course
covariance = np.cov(tcs, maruti, ddof=0)[0, 1]
correlation = np.corrcoef(tcs, maruti)[0, 1]

print(f"Covariance: {covariance:.4f}")
print(f"Correlation: {correlation:.4f}")
# Covariance: 1.0833
# Correlation: 0.3205
body.caption: np.corrcoef() is scale-invariant, so it gives the same answer regardless of ddof. np.cov() needs ddof=0 to match this course's formulas.
Rough guide to correlation magnitude (not a precise rule, judgement still matters)

Chapter 1's single-sector banking portfolio, assumed at 0.65
TCS and Maruti Suzuki, this lesson's 0.32
Chapter 1's multi-sector assumption of 0.35 sits just above this band
Genuinely rare between two Indian large-cap equities in the same market

body.text: Notice the last row's caveat. Two equities listed on the same exchange usually share a common market factor, moves driven by FII flows, interest rate expectations, and overall risk appetite, so genuinely negative correlations between large-cap Indian stocks are unusual. Meaningfully negative correlation is easier to find across asset classes, for instance between equities and gold during a flight to safety, than between two stocks in the same market.

children.text: From a Pair to a Grid: the Covariance Matrix

markDefs.definition: A square grid listing the variance of each asset along the diagonal and the covariance of every pair of assets off the diagonal. For N assets, it is an N by N grid.

children.text: With two assets, one covariance number is all there is. Add a third stock, and there are now three pairs to track. Add ten stocks, and there are forty-five pairs. The standard way to organize this is the
: each asset's own variance sits on the diagonal, since an asset's covariance with itself is just its variance, and every pairwise covariance sits in its own cell off the diagonal.

body.caption: The 2x2 covariance matrix for TCS and Maruti Suzuki

children.text: The matrix is symmetric, since Cov(TCS, Maruti) always equals Cov(Maruti, TCS). Lesson 3 of this chapter builds this same grid for five stocks at once, and it is exactly this matrix that Chapter 3's portfolio optimization runs on. Nothing conceptually new happens at ten, fifty, or five hundred stocks. The grid just gets bigger.
A Practical Warning: Correlation Is Not Stable

body.text: Six months of data is enough to demonstrate the formula, not enough to trust the number. A correlation estimated from a handful of observations swings around a lot from one sample to the next. Practitioners generally lean on at least two to three years of history, roughly 24 to 36 monthly observations or several hundred daily ones, before treating a correlation estimate as reasonably stable, and even then it is re-estimated on a rolling basis rather than fixed forever.

children.text: There is a second, sharper problem than sample size. Correlations are not constant even when correctly measured over a long window, they shift with the market regime. Chapter 1 mentioned that correlations across sectors spike toward 1 during a panic. TCS and Maruti Suzuki's calm 0.32 is a normal-times number. In a systemic sell-off like March 2020, expect that number to climb well above its long-run average, right when low correlation would have been most valuable.

body.title: Compute a covariance from deviations
body.prompt: Two stocks, X and Y, each had 5 months of returns. Their deviations from their own means were: X: 2, -3, 3, 0, -2. Y: 1, -2, 2, -3, 2 (same months, in order). What is Cov(X, Y)?

body.title: Turn that covariance into a correlation
body.prompt: Using the covariance you just computed (2.0), along with X's standard deviation of 2.28% and Y's standard deviation of 2.10%, compute the correlation between X and Y.
body.explanation: Correlation = Cov(X, Y) / (std_X x std_Y) = 2.0 / (2.28 x 2.10) = 2.0 / 4.788 = 0.418, or roughly 0.42.

body.title: Choosing a pair for risk reduction
body.question: You are building a 2-stock portfolio purely to minimize risk. Pair A has a correlation of 0.85. Pair B has a correlation of 0.15. Individual stock volatilities are similar in both pairs. Which pair gives more diversification benefit?
options: Pair A, because higher correlation always means safer combinations
Pair B, because its lower correlation lets the two stocks' swings cancel each other out more
Both pairs give identical diversification benefit, since correlation does not affect portfolio risk
It is impossible to say without knowing each stock's expected return
body.explanation: Lower correlation means the two stocks' good and bad months line up less often, so combining them cancels out more of each one's individual swings. Pair B, at 0.15, offers meaningfully more diversification benefit than Pair A at 0.85, all else equal. Chapter 2's remaining lessons turn this into an exact number for portfolio variance.

cards.definition: The average product of two assets' deviations from their own means, in the same periods. Positive if they tend to move together, negative if they tend to move apart. Measured in percent-squared.
Covariance divided by the product of the two assets' standard deviations. Always between -1 and +1, and unit-free, which makes it comparable across any pair of assets.
A square grid holding every asset's variance on the diagonal and every pairwise covariance off the diagonal. The input to portfolio-level risk calculations for any number of assets.

points: Covariance measures whether two assets' returns tend to move together (positive), apart (negative), or show no clear pattern (near zero), but its percent-squared units are hard to interpret directly.
Correlation rescales covariance by both standard deviations, producing a unit-free number always between -1 and +1 that is directly comparable across any pair of assets.
TCS and Maruti Suzuki's correlation, worked out in full this lesson, is 0.32: positive but loose, exactly the kind of relationship that produced Chapter 1's surprising risk result.
Genuinely negative correlation between two large-cap Indian equities is rare, since most stocks in the same market share exposure to the same broad market factor.
For more than two assets, pairwise covariances are organized into a covariance matrix, with variances on the diagonal. This is the direct input to the portfolio optimization in Chapter 3.
Correlation estimates need a reasonable sample size to be trustworthy, and they are not fixed. They tend to rise sharply during market panics, right when low correlation matters most.
